newsitem.title: USA: Simpson lawyers denied appeal in civil trial.
newsitem.headline: Simpson lawyers denied appeal in civil trial.

text.p: An appeal by O.J. Simpson's attorneys against key rulings by the judge in the football hero's civil trial was rejected on Monday, effectively gagging his defence team's attack on police in the case.
In its ruling the California Court of Appeals said Simpson's defence team had "failed to demonstrate entitlement to extraordinary relief."
In making its ruling the appellate court also automatically denied Simpson's defence its request to halt the trial while it considered the appeal.

In their appeal writ, Simpson's defence team said Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki had "abused (his) discretion" by not allowing them to pursue their theory that police bungled, contaminated and planted evidence in a conspiracy to frame him.

The writ, filed late on Friday afternoon in the California State Court of Appeals in Los Angeles, said Simpson "will be irreparably harmed if he is required to go through the entire trial not being allowed to cross-examine (police) witnesses as to their credibility and lack of proper police procedures employed by the Los Angeles Police Department."

Fujisaki's rulings, made during pre-trial hearings and last Monday when lawyers for the plaintiffs in the case presented their first police witnesses, prevented defence lawyers from delving into aspects of the case that they claimed showed a conspiracy to frame Simpson or at the very least, demonstrated a bungled police investgation and a "rush to justice."
Simpson was found not guilty by a criminal court jury in October 1995 of the June 12, 1994, murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman.
He is being sued in civil court for damages by the families of the victims in a wrongful death case and could be forced to pay them millions of dollars if found responsible for the murders.

Simpson's civil trial attorneys, headed by Robert Baker, have been repeatedly frustrated in their cross-examinations of police witnesses as lawyers for the plaintiffs have successfully objected to questions casting doubt on the competency and honesty of officers.

Their writ asked the appeals court to "command" Fujisaki to allow "full cross-examination of (plaintiffs') witnesses including examination on credibility, examination on police procedures and examination on the failure to collect evidence and what they did not do in their investigation of these murders."
The document also requested that, "As this trial is ongoing, an immediate stay of the proceedings should (be ordered) until this matter can be ruled upon."

The ongoing battle between Baker and Fujisaki came to a head last Monday when the judge ruled that evidence documented but not collected by police, including a scrap of paper found next to the bodies, blood that was not taken from Nicole Simpson's back, and an eyeglass lens that was lost by the LAPD crime lab, could not be used by the defence to prove police incompetence or any theory that officers conspired to frame Simpson.

"This is not a case against the LAPD for committing malpractice, the defendant is not suing the LAPD. Whether or not the police department did or did not act within certain protocols of investigation is immaterial," Fujisaki ruled.
Baker, appearing angry, said, "I disagree with the court's ruling."
Baker then asked for a halt in the court proceedings in order to file an appeal and the judge refused the request.
Meanwhile, the civil case jury heard an expert testify on Monday that routine blood tests linked Simpson to the murders before more sophisticated DNA testing was performed.

Greg Matheson, a supervisor at the Los Angeles Police Department's crime lab, testifying as the trial entered its scientific phase, said Simpson's blood and enzyme groupings matched blood found at the murder scene outside Nicole Simpson's condominium and at his mansion nearby. Those groupings, he said, were shared by only about one in 570 people in the population.
In Simpson's criminal trial experts testified that subsequent DNA tests showed the chances of the blood belonging to anyone other than Simpson were several billion to one.
